title: Appraisal Fraud and Illegal Property Flipping: Detecting Inflated Values Before the Loan Funds
summary: Collateral fraud is the most expensive kind a lender can fund, because the loss lands on a property that was never worth the loan. How value inflation, cherry-picked comparables, condition misrepresentation, edited photos and flip chains show up in a mortgage file, what FHA's anti-flipping rule at 24 CFR 203.37a and appraiser independence under Regulation Z require, and the collateral checks an AI agent can run on every appraisal rather than a sample.
body_markdown:
## The Fraud That Sets the Size of the Loss


When a borrower overstates income, the loan may default. When the collateral is overstated, the loan is worse than that: if it defaults, the property behind it was never worth what was lent, and the loss is the gap. Collateral fraud is the category where a lender's exposure is decided at origination, by a number in the appraisal, and nothing in servicing can recover what was never there.


Collateral fraud is also often organised. A single borrower inflating income is usually acting alone. Inflating a value usually takes more than one participant: a seller who bought low, an appraiser willing to reach a number, sometimes a loan officer or broker applying pressure, and a buyer who may or may not know. That is part of what makes it detectable. Several people leave several traces, in the appraisal, the title history and the transaction.


We have written about the legitimate side of collateral review,[AVM quality control and reconsiderations of value](https://www.seiright.com/blog/ai-collateral-desk-avm-quality-control-rule-reconsideration-of-value-appraisal-independence) and[when an appraisal can be waived](https://www.seiright.com/blog/value-acceptance-appraisal-waiver-ai-collateral-decisioning-rep-and-warrant) . This post is about the schemes, and the signals in the file that give them away.


## Value Inflation and the Comparables That Support It


An appraised value is an argument built from comparable sales, and an inflated value is a bad argument made to look like a good one. The most common technique is selective comparables: choosing sales that are farther away, larger, newer or in a better location than the subject, and then making adjustments too small to close the gap.


The signals are in the appraisal itself and in what it left out:


- **Distance and similarity.** Comparables many miles away in a market where closer sales exist, especially in a different town or school district, need a stated reason. A file where three of five comparables are over twenty miles from the subject is worth a reviewer's look even when every adjustment looks reasonable.
- **Adjustment patterns.** Net and gross adjustment percentages well above the levels the GSEs expect, adjustments in the wrong direction (a superior feature on the comparable should reduce its adjusted price, not raise it) and per-square-foot adjustments that do not match the market all suggest the comparables are carrying more than they should.
- **The value lands exactly on the contract price.** It happens legitimately. When an appraiser's work does so far more often than their peers', or when the value lands exactly on the price on a file with weak comparables, it suggests the appraisal was written to reach a number.
- **Disagreement with the reports already in the file.** Fannie Mae's Collateral Underwriter and Freddie Mac's Loan Collateral Advisor return risk scores and messages through the Uniform Collateral Data Portal, and many lenders also pull an AVM. When the appraised value sits well above the AVM and the GSE collateral tools flag overvaluation risk, the agent reads the reports, puts the value beside them, and states the gap with the comparables that drive it.


A finding here is usually a review, not a fail. Distant comparables can be the only comparables in a rural market. The point is that a reviewer sees the specific weakness, with the page cited, and can order a desk review or a second appraisal on the files that need one, rather than sampling ten percent and hoping the inflated ones were in the sample.


## Condition Misrepresentation: The Defect That Was in the Report


The other way to overstate collateral is to overstate its condition. Here the fraud, or the error, is often visible in the appraisal itself: the appraiser describes a problem in the comments and does not carry it into the condition rating or the value.


An appraisal can rate a property C3, with no repairs required and an "as is" value, while the comments mention an active roof leak, water in the basement, foundation cracking or a missing handrail on the stairs. The photographs can show peeling paint on a house built before 1978, which matters for FHA's lead-based paint requirements, or damage the narrative never mentions. Agency repurchases in this category very often turn out to involve a defect that was in the file and nobody read.


The check is a reconciliation: extract every defect the appraiser described anywhere in the report, look at every photograph for visible condition problems, and compare both against the condition rating, the "as is" or "subject to" basis and the required repairs. A defect disclosed in the comments, behind a clean rating and an unconditioned value, is a finding regardless of whether anyone intended it.


## Photos That Are Not of This House, or Not as It Is


Appraisal photographs are evidence, and evidence can be edited. The schemes range from reusing photos from a prior listing, taken before the property deteriorated, to photographing a different house, to editing out a car, a dumpster, a damaged section of siding or a neighbouring eyesore. Generative editing tools now make the last of these a few seconds' work.


The checks that help:


- **Compare against the other photos in the package.** Loan files often contain the same property in several places: the appraisal, the listing, an inspection, an earlier appraisal. A photo that matches a listing photo from years earlier, or that differs from another copy of itself in the file, is a finding.
- **Read the file behind the image.** Capture dates that predate the inspection, location data that does not match the property, and the editing traces that generative tools leave around a changed region are all evidence about whether a photo is current and unaltered.
- **Compare what the photo shows with what the report says.** A photo of a sound roof and a narrative describing a new roof agree. A photo of a damaged roof and a C2 rating do not.


## Illegal Flipping: Appreciation Nothing Explains


Buying a property and reselling it at a profit is legal and common. Illegal flipping is a resale at an inflated price, supported by a fraudulent appraisal, fabricated or overstated renovations, or a buyer who is a straw purchaser, so the profit comes from the lender rather than from the property. Flip chains move a property through a sequence of related buyers, each at a higher price, to manufacture a sales history that supports the final value.


FHA addresses this directly. Under[24 CFR 203.37a](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-24/subtitle-B/chapter-II/subchapter-B/part-203/subpart-A/section-203.37a) , a property resold within 90 days of the seller's acquisition is not eligible for an FHA-insured mortgage, and a resale between 91 and 180 days at a price 100% or more above what the seller paid requires additional documentation, including a second appraisal. HUD has issued time-limited waivers of parts of this rule in the past, so the current status should be confirmed against HUD's guidance. Conventional programs have no equivalent bright line, but the same facts are the risk signal.


The signals, all available from the file and the title history:


- **Days since the seller acquired the property, and the price they paid.** The title commitment and the appraisal's prior-sale history both carry this.
- **Appreciation against the market.** A property that has risen far more than local prices over the same period needs an explanation.
- **Evidence of real renovation.** A large price increase on a "fully renovated" property should be supported by the appraisal's description and photos and, where available, permits. An increase with no visible work behind it is the classic illegal flip.
- **Who the seller is.** A seller that is an LLC formed shortly before acquiring the property, or one whose officers, address or registered agent match another party to the transaction, is a reason to look harder at the price.
- **The prior sale's nature.** An acquisition at a foreclosure auction, a short sale or a sale between related parties sets a low base that a quick resale may legitimately exceed, or may be exploiting.


## Appraiser Independence Is Part of the Fraud Picture


Some collateral fraud starts with pressure on the appraiser.[Regulation Z's valuation independence rule at 12 CFR 1026.42](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/chapter-X/part-1026/subpart-E/section-1026.42) prohibits coercing or influencing an appraiser to misstate a value, and prohibits extending credit on a valuation the creditor knows was affected by that conduct, unless the creditor uses reasonable diligence to determine the value is not materially misstated. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac apply their own appraiser independence requirements on top of that.


This matters for detection because evidence of pressure sometimes sits in the file: an email or message asking the appraiser to "hit the number," a request for reconsideration that supplies only higher-priced comparables with no basis, or a pattern of revised appraisals that move value upward after the first version came in low. An agent reading the whole file can surface those alongside the valuation findings, so the reviewer sees both the weak comparables and the pressure that may have produced them.


## The Honest Read


Collateral fraud is the hardest category to undo after funding and one of the most visible before it, because the evidence is in the appraisal, the photos and the title history the lender already has. The signals are specific: comparables that skip closer and cheaper sales, defects in the comments that never reached the rating, photos that do not match the property as it is, and appreciation that no renovation or market movement explains.


An agent does not replace an appraiser or a review appraiser, and it does not produce a value. What the[Fraud Agent](https://www.seiright.com/for-lenders/fraud-agent) does is read every appraisal and every photo in the file, put the value beside the reports already there, check the sale history, and route the weak cases to the people who decide, with the reason and the page attached. The full list of collateral and valuation schemes we target is in our[mortgage fraud guide](https://www.seiright.com/blog/guides/mortgage-fraud#collateral) .
